articles.title: He Invented Courtroom Theater, Then Took His Act To Star Trek
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

What attorney was crowned “the King of Torts” by Life magazine in 1954, this flamboyant San Francisco trial lawyer transformed personal-injury law by wheeling scale models, films, and even a client’s severed prosthetic leg in front of juries, earning a second nickname, “the Father of Demonstrative Evidence”? His celebrity client list ran from Errol Flynn and Mae West to Muhammad Ali and the Rolling Stones, and he defended Jack Ruby for free.

Hint: He also, improbably, had a memorable acting turn as an alien on Star Trek.

articles.title: How To Create Evergreen Resource Libraries That Dominate Search
articles.content:
Evergreen content is the foundation of a strong law firm website because it provides information that remains relevant and useful to potential clients over time. The most effective resource libraries are organized around content hubs or pillars that connect related pages, helping search engines understand the site’s structure and boosting visibility in search results. For human users, you will probably also want to create a “resource library” page that organizes links to individual pieces of content by topic and content type (e.g., how-to guides, legal definitions). A well-organized, consistently maintained archive of evergreen resources not only improves your law firm website’s performance in search results, but also helps to build trust with potential clients and establish your law firm website itself as a go-to resource for questions in your practice area.
Evergreen content is material posted to your law firm website that retains its value over time. This retention of value needs to be calibrated both by the consistency of the information itself (statutory definitions and rules of procedure will normally qualify; a discussion of cases currently on a district court’s docket usually would not) and by the consistency of the searches potential clients run to find that information (”grounds for divorce in Mississippi” would count, but “Easter egg hunts on public property” would not).
Those topical parameters help to establish what evergreen means, but ideally you (and your content strategy team) should be putting some thought into defining resources, as well. How-to guides, “complete guide to…” articles, and checklists to prepare for various legal scenarios can all be valuable types of resources when linked with topics of consistent interest to your client base. Commentary unpacking the implications of recent court decisions may not be, even if they serve valuable functions elsewhere (these can be great for podcast appearances!).
If you want to create evergreen content that outperforms the topical coverage of competitive law firms because it is “better,” you will need to put some consideration into defining what better means in the context of your law practice and your content strategy. The conventional wisdom for creating “better” content is to pick a competitor whose website is ranking higher than search engine results pages (SERPs) than yours is and try to push past their content on several key metrics. The metrics you choose to emphasize can make all the difference in how this approach plays out for you.
One of the most crucial elements of a beat-your-competition strategy for evergreen content is to simply create more of it than other law firms are offering. Sometimes there is a tendency to think of “more” purely in terms of word count, or number of pages/posts hosted on your law firm website. That’s a missed opportunity. To get more from your “more,” develop a plan for building out your evergreen content library that frames “more” in two related ways:
You are looking for ways to increase the number of angles from which you examine a topic or the number of perspectives from which you explain it, and you are aiming to maximize the level of detail with which you develop coverage from each point of entry.
If you don’t yet have a clearly-defined content hub on your law firm website, your evergreen resource library gives you a great opportunity to create one. Technically, you could create the resource library using any structure you liked, or simply by posting a series of standalone pages that each provided thorough topical coverage of the legal issues they addressed. However, organizing your resource library in this way fails to take advantage of one of the most powerful tools for helping search and answer engines make sense of your law firm website and (therefore) recognize when to show users your content in response to a search query.
I like to recommend starting with a content hub or pillar because a content pillar is usually going to consist of content that will be “evergreen” anyway, and because building out a pillar or hub structure sets you up to tackle every facet of your chosen topic from multiple angles. By organizing your resource library as a content pillar, you position the relevance of the items in that library to register with search engine indexing bots. The “map” of your website shows Google (and other search tools) how the pieces of evergreen content relate to each other both vertically and laterally, so the result is that search tools are able to consider the entire hub in determining the quality of your law firm website and the relevance of its content to a user’s search query.
Another way in which you can outstrip your competitors is in the selection of keywords you target. There are two ways to think about keyword selection for evergreen resource libraries.
The first way is in making sure you are hitting the big, generalist terms that are sure to show up repeatedly in searches by people looking for the kinds of legal services your law firm offers, month after month. Often these variations on the name of your practice area, or a legal requirement (e.g., “court-ordered mediation”) that commonly affects the kinds of cases you handle. The good news here is that content designed to target these keywords will almost always be relevant; the bad news is that even high-quality, extremely relevant content may have trouble getting ahead of the competition simply because there is so much content out there, jockeying for eyeballs and clicks.
The second way is to focus on identifying long-tail keywords that clearly correspond to a very specific legal question that most of your competitors are not answering, or only answering shallowly. Then write (or have your content team write) content that answers each question directly and comprehensively. Be prepared for the fact that to use this approach to keyword targeting effectively you will need to answer a lot of questions, probably more than you think. On the other hand, the process of answering them will mean that you are also fulfilling the goal of covering your topic from multiple angles we discussed earlier.
Even after you target high-competition and low-competition keywords, there are bound to be at least a few competitors covering most of the same topics your website addresses; they are working in the same area of law, after all. Talk with your digital marketing team to try and make sure that you are not competing against exactly the same handful of websites across all targeted keywords. Remember that part of the goal is to ensure that your evergreen resources are more comprehensive than those of competitors. If you are competing on all keywords, but not against all of the same firms for each keyword, this is a good sign that your resource library is covering a wider range of subtopics related to your practice area than most of your competitors are covering individually.
The exact details will depend on the scope of your planned resource library and the topical and type-of-content categories that make sense to you and your content team Organizing your content in terms of categories that your clients themselves use in conceptualizing their legal concerns can often give you a boost in matching search relevance and in helping your website visitors recognize what they are seeing, so that they find navigating your website to be an intuitive process that puts them at ease, rather than an additional source of stress and confusion in their search for reliable legal information. However, you also want to make sure that you develop a framework for organizing your evergreen resource library that makes it easy for you and the team managing your website to see where new content fits into your established categories so that the library as a whole maintains a consistent organizational structure, even as you add content to it over time.
Once you have your evergreen content library set up and ready for visitors, you will want to keep it “fresh.” That might sound like a contradiction in terms, but the idea here is to make updates as needed, when the laws in your state change or when new court decisions affect how cases are likely to be handled during litigation. Remove any content that is misleadingly out-of-date as soon as possible, and work with your digital marketing team to create new content that adds new answers to familiar questions as time goes by.
Building an evergreen resource library is not about publishing more content for the sake of volume. It is about creating a comprehensive, well-organized collection of legal resources that consistently answers the questions your prospective clients are asking. When supported by a strategic content hub structure, thoughtful keyword targeting, and ongoing maintenance, an evergreen library can become one of the most valuable assets on your law firm website. Whether you develop it in-house or partner with an experienced legal marketing agency, investing in evergreen resources today can help your firm attract qualified traffic, build authority, and generate leads for years to come.
Annette Choti, Esq., has over two decades of legal experience and is the Founder & CEO of Law Quill, a concierge legal marketing agency for law firms. Annette authored the bestselling book Click Magnet: The Ultimate Guide To Digital Marketing For Law Firms, hosts the popular Legal Marketing Lounge podcast, and founded Click Magnet Academy where she teaches professionals to leverage the powerful LinkedIn platform. As a sought after speaker for Bar Associations, Legal Associations, and Marketing Conferences, Annette provides legal marketing insight along with an entertaining twist. Annette used to do theatre and professional comedy, which is not so different from the legal field if we are all being honest. articles.title: Trump DOJ Considers Mission To Exonerate Richard Nixon
articles.content:
According to the Wall Street Journal, a senior Justice Department official invited an 81-year-old Dick Nixon deadender to headquarters to spend two hours walking the Office of Professional Responsibility through a lengthy slidedeck he created called “Watergate As Lawfare.” Geoff Shepard, who worked on Nixon’s defense team, continues to bang a drum more than a half century hence that the deep state took down Richard Nixon. Justice Department historically rolled their eyes at his theories, but the crackerjack team that Todd Blanche oversees is now conducting a preliminary review into whether the Watergate special prosecutors committed misconduct.
The Trump DOJ… laser-focused on the issues impacting America in 2026.
Officially, the Justice Department says Shepard was invited for his scholarship — a term used highly loosely — and “that presentation does not constitute an investigation.” On the other hand, the DOJ historically isn’t in the business of granting two-hour interviews on matters where they aren’t already deeply invested.
The statement also misspelled Shepard’s name, befitting the attention to detail that we’ve come to expect out of the gang that couldn’t shoot straight over at Justice.
Launching a bid to exonerate Nixon — at least indirectly via besmirching the reputation of the special prosecutors involved — runs somewhat afoul of the fact that Nixon never got charged. A grand jury named him an unindicted co-conspirator and impeachment proceedings loomed on the horizon, but Nixon resigned and ran away from office rather than take his chances with whatever defense Shepard and his team cooked up. A month later, Gerald Ford pardoned Nixon, which the former president accepted knowing that, per Burdick v. United States, that pardon “carries an imputation of guilt.”
So whatever review the DOJ embarks upon can’t clear Nixon, only cast aspersions upon the special prosecutors, Archibald Cox and Leon Jaworski, who died in 2004 and 1982. At the same time that the DOJ asserts authority to short-circuit all ethical inquiries into government lawyers, they may be firing up a crusade to go after dead prosecutors over a case from the early 70s. Ironically, the Office of Professional Responsibility — the somewhat ironically named body at the center of this story — only exists because of Watergate, having been set up in 1975 as part of a wide-swath of reforms designed to keep any future president from doing what Nixon did.
Shepard argues that special prosecutors met secretly with judges and sat on evidence the defense should have seen. Due process matters, but on June 23, 1972, six days after the break-in, Nixon taped himself signing off on a plan to have the CIA wave the FBI off the investigation, and you can’t blame any ex parte meeting for that. The Supreme Court ruled unanimously that Nixon had to turn those recordings over. Shepard, as it happens, helped supervise the transcription of those tapes, with their notorious lengthy audio gaps.
To be clear, as the definitive Nixon obituary put it, “he was scum.” There is no question of his guilt. In a move that would shame Stringer Bell, he even recorded himself doing crimes.
And yet, the administration’s revisionist history machine is in full swing. We should have seen this coming in June, when JD Vance went to the Nixon Library and joked that if Watergate happened tomorrow, “it would be like a 12-hour news story.” He followed it up by invoking the “deep state” and comparing Nixon’s downfall to what this deep state tried to do to Trump. Just as this DOJ story broke, Rep. Riley Moore told a Nixon Foundation audience that Nixon was “absolutely couped out of office and was framed,” and that Nixon knew it the whole time, but kept quiet to protect public confidence in American institutions.
That noble silence was probably what got deleted in that 18-minute audio gap.
Why Nixon? Why now? On one level, this caps off a long-time mission of the conservative legal movement. While it presents as an intellectual project draped in originalism and unitary executive theory, it’s just the byproduct of a bunch of late 70s Republicans fluffing up a pseudo legal justification to bring back segregation and clear Richard Nixon. It’s not an accident that Antonin Scalia’s first big assignment running the Office of Legal Counsel in 1974 was concluding that the tapes were Nixon’s personal property. Unitary executive theory touches on a wide array of executive functions, but at its root it’s just “when the president does it, that means that it is not illegal” run through an English-to-Legalese dictionary.
On another level, though, this is about throwing $6.00 gasoline on the Trump v. United States fire. It’s one thing to clear Trump of his first term crimes, and another to build the scaffolding for getting him out of the next wave of special prosecutions. If the DOJ goes forward with half century delinquent thought experiment, whatever report they belch out will be a roman à clef that will make Animal Farm look subtle. Just cross out Cox and Jaworski, and write in whichever lawyer becomes the next poor sap who has to deal with America’s dumbest charlatans asking about Iowa games.
If Richard Nixon broke the heart of the American dream, then the conservative legal movement and its Trumpian distillation track the toxic masculine response to heartbreak. The aggressive refusal to accept responsibility that hardens into a manicured worldview designed to justify their contemptuous revenge tour against anyone they can blame for their own failures. They are America’s most despicable ex-boyfriend, having traded bodyspray for a Federalist Society membership card.
Joe Patrice is a senior editor at Above the Law and co-host of Thinking Like A Lawyer. Feel free to email any tips, questions, or comments. Follow him on Twitter or Bluesky if you’re interested in law, politics, and a healthy dose of college sports news.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy’s Defense Suffers Setback After Mistrial
articles.content:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.
It’s not new rocket science by any means. It’s the fact that they cannot prove probable cause.
— Kevin Reddington, an attorney for Lindsay Clancy, arguing that prosecutors failed to establish that his client was criminally responsible for the deaths of her three children because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time. Clancy’s first trial ended in a mistrial after the jury deadlocked 11–1 in favor of finding her not guilty by reason of insanity. A judge has since declined to acquit her outright, ruling that prosecutors presented enough evidence for a rational jury to find her guilty.
Staci Zaretsky is the managing editor of Above the Law, where she’s worked since 2011. She’d love to hear from you, so please feel free to email her with any tips, questions, comments, or critiques. You can follow her on Bluesky, X/Twitter, and Threads, or connect with her on LinkedIn.
